41Python Interface

This chapter discusses the Python interface that can be used to create customized
device simulation flows. This feature is available with a license.

Overview of Python Interface

       The simulation capabilities of Sentaurus Device are available as a Python module that can
       be loaded into the Python interpreter gpythonsh (see SentaurusTM Workbench User Guide,
       gpythonsh). You can use the Python interface to create advanced simulation flows that can
       utilize the multitude of available Python packages and frameworks.

       The Sentaurus Device Python interface consists of many classes that allow device
       simulations to be constructed in a pythonic manner. The general structure and syntax of the
       Sentaurus Device command file is represented by a group of classes so that the simulation
       is set up in a more object-oriented fashion.

       When using the interactive Python interpreter, gpythonsh, general help documentation for
       the module can be read by entering:

          import sentaurus.device as sd
          help(sd)

       When using modern IDEs, such as Visual Studio Code, the Python interface takes
       advantage of interactive intellisense features such as auto-completion and inline
       documentation. HTML documentation of all functions and classes are also available from
       the Sentaurus Workbench Help > Python API Documentation > S-Device menu or under
       $STROOT/current/manuals/sdevice_api/index.html. The STROOT environment
       variable indicates where the Synopsys TCAD distribution has been installed.

       The Python interface can be used interactively or in batch mode by passing a Python script
       with Sentaurus Device commands to the general-purpose Python shell:

          gpythonsh <Sentaurus Device_Python_command_script>

       For a richer experience, you also can use the Python interface interactively with IPython,
       which is distributed as part of the general-purpose Python shell:

          gpythonsh -m IPython

SentaurusTM Device User Guide                                                      1549
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
Performing Device Simulations

Performing Device Simulations

       The first step in setting up a device simulation is to create an instance of the Device class
       describing the device to be simulated. The following simple example shows how this can be
       done:

          from sentaurus.device import *
          device = Device(

             file = File(grid = "diode.tdr", plot = "diode_sim",
                                   current = "diode_sim"),

             electrodes = [
                 Electrode(name="anode", voltage=1),
                 Electrode(name="cathode", voltage=0)

             ],
             physics = Physics(

               mobility = Mobility(doping_dependence=DopingDependence(),
                                                    high_field_saturation=True),

               recombination = Recombination(srh=SRH(doping_dependence=True))
             )
          )

       The device is defined by specifying the information like what is normally added to the
       command file, but in a Python-like way. Some points to note are:

       · In the standard command file syntax, a Device section is created only if a mixed-mode
            simulation is being created. When using the Python interface, an instance of the Device
            class is always created, even in single device simulations.

       · When constructing the device, Python objects that correspond to the different sections of
            the command file are created, for example, File, Math, Physics objects corresponding
            to File, Math and Physics sections.

       · In the example, only a single Physics section is created. Multiple sections are created
            by creating multiple Physics objects inside a Python list, for example, physics = [
            Physics(...), Physics(...) ]. The Physics section is later on accessible under the
            property physics as a dictionary, where the region or material property of the
            Physics section is used as key. The global Physics section has "global" as key.
            Instead of a list, it is also possible to pass in a dictionary {"physics1": Physics(...)},
            in which case the explicitly defined keys "physics1" are used to access them.

       After creating Device instances, an instance of the SimulationSetup class is created:

          setup = SimulationSetup(
             devices = device,
             global_file = GlobalFile(output="diode_sim"),
             global_math = GlobalMath(exit_on_failure=True)

          )

       This class describes all the information required to set up the simulation:

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1550
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
Performing Device Simulations

       · In this case, a single device simulation is created, but multi-device simulations are
            created by creating multiple Device instances and passing them in a Python list, for
            example, devices=[device1, device2].

       · Instances of GlobalFile and GlobalMath classes can be created to define the global
            settings for these sections. In the standard command file syntax, only File and Math
            sections exist and there are certain parameters in these sections that can be defined only
            at the global level and device level. This is documented in this user guide, but this
            separation of the GlobalFile and GlobalMath classes from the device-specific File
            and Math classes makes this distinction clearer.

       Once a SimulationSetup instance has been created, an instance of the Simulation class
       can be created to run the actual simulation, as follows:

          sim = Simulation(setup)
          state = sim.solve(

             Coupled(equations=[Equation.Poisson], iterations=10),
             Coupled(equations=[Equation.Poisson, Equation.Electron,

                                                Equation.Hole])),
             QuasiStationary(

                 do_zero=True, initial_step=0.1, max_step=0.1, min_step=0.1,
                 goal=Goal(name="anode", voltage=2),
                 solve_cmd=Coupled(equations=[Equation.Poisson,

                                                                      Equation.Electron,
                                                                      Equation.Hole]))
          )

       In this example, the Simulation object is created and a simple quasistationary ramp is run
       (after a couple of initial Coupled simulations). In this simulation, the solve method of the
       Simulation class is used to perform the simulation. This method has the following features:

       · This is equivalent to the Solve section in the standard command file syntax and the
            statements that usually appear in the Solve section have equivalent classes in the
            Python interface.

       · When calling the solve method, callback functions can be passed in that are called
            during various stages of the simulation.

       · The function returns a SimulationState object. This is a largely opaque object that can
            be used to restore the simulation state later in the simulation using Simulation's load
            method.

       · In the event of a convergence failure, this function reports a SolveError exception.

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1551
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
Accessing Simulation Results

Accessing Simulation Results

Aside from the normal file output of the simulation results, the results generated by the

simulation can be accessed from within Python via the result property of the Simulation
class.

Accessing this property returns a Pandas DataFrame containing all the current and device
plot results. Pandas is a third-party Python package that is the gold standard for data

analysis in Python. It is an extremely powerful package that provides a huge range of

functionality for accessing and manipulating data.

In the simplest case, a Pandas DataFrame can be thought of as a table where the rows are
time points in the simulation and columns are the data sets of current plot data, such as

"drain OuterVoltage".

The simple example below shows some very basic usage:

 # Get the Pandas DataFrame containing all simulation results
 res = sim.result

# Get the columns for the gate voltage and drain current
vg = res["gate OuterVoltage"]
id = res["drain TotalCurrent"]

# Get the most recent values of gate voltage and drain current
v = vg.iloc[-1]
I = id.iloc[-1]

If the NewCurrentPrefix feature is used in the simulation, the prefix is added to the data
frame as a separate column. In Pandas, the data for the times in the simulation
corresponding to a given current prefix can be filtered as follows:

 # Filter the results to get the data frame that contains all rows
 # that correspond to the current prefix "ramp1"
 res = sim.result
 res_ramp1 = res[res["prefix"] == "ramp1"]

Aside from the current plot data, the results data frame also contains objects representing

snapshots of the device state that were created by plot statements. The DeviceSnapshot
class encapsulates the 2D/3D internal field data of the device, for example, electron density.

The snapshot objects appear in the rows at the time point they were plotted, allowing for
easy correlation between a device snapshot and a data point in the current plot data. For
example:

# This picks out the row for time 0.5  and then reads the gate
# voltage, drain current and gets the  corresponding device snapshot
res = sim.result
row = res[res["time"] == 0.5]
vg = row["gate OuterVoltage"].iloc[0]

SentaurusTM Device User Guide                                         1552

          sn = row["DeviceSnapshot"].iloc[0]

Using Time Step Callback in Solve

       The solve method of the Simulation class has an optional named argument called
       timestep_callback. It allows you to inject a user-defined Python method, which is called
       after each time step, in a Quasistationary or Transient statement. The callback can be
       used to access the simulation state and to break out of the current Quasistationary or
       Transient statement as well as execute any other Python code. As such,
       timestep_callback provides capabilities that are not available in a standard Sentaurus
       Device simulation and allows for complex simulation flows.

       In the callback function, you have access to simulation data such as information about the
       last Quasistationary or Transient step, simulation statistics (see also SimStats in
       Simulation Statistics for Plotting and Output on page 231 and full access to the simulation
       results up to that time.

       The first argument of the callback function is the Simulation object for the simulation, and
       the second argument is an object of the TimestepInfo class, which provides access to the
       respective TransientTimestepInfo or QuasistatTimestepInfor object and the
       SimStats object.

       The TimestepInfo object has the request_break() method to inform the program to
       return from the current Quasistationary or Transient statement even if the specified goal
       has not yet been reached. This is analogous to the static BreakCriteria specified in the
       Math section. An optional string argument allows you to specify a custom message, which
       is printed to the log file as the reason for ending the current Quasistationary or Transient
       statement.

       Note:

           You can specify both the static BreakCriteria in the Math section and a dynamic
           break criterion using timestep_callback of the solve() method at the same
           time.

       You can use the help() method to obtain detailed information about the simulation state
       accessible through the TimestepInfo class. For example, use
       help(sdevice.TransientTimestepInfo).

       The following code snippet shows how to return from the current Quasistationary
       statement if the outer voltage of the drain has exceeded a certain value and how to initiate
       a device plot:

          # Define callback for break criterion
          def timestep_callback(sim, solve):

             print("timestep_callback:", solve.info.total_time,
                        solve.info.step, solve.info.converged, flush=True)

SentaurusTM Device User Guide                     1553
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface

res = sim.result

   solve.request_break("timestep_callback:
                                           > 1.5")

Using the Plugin Step Callback in Solve

       Similar to timestep_callback, the solve() method of the Simulation class has the
       option solver_callback, which allows you to insert a user-defined Python method that is
       called after each plugin iteration.

       In the callback function, you have access to all the information accessible for timestep
       callback functions. In addition, you have access to information related to plugin iterations,
       including the current iteration number, the equation error of the current and previous
       iterations, and whether all the solves in the finished iteration have converged.

       The usage of the plugin step callback function is similar to the timestep callback function.
       There is an additional option keep_solution in the request_break() function, which
       controls whether the following solve() calls continue from the solutions calculated from the
       plugin iterations. By default, keep_solution is false.

       The following code snippet shows how to implement a hybrid solve method, which starts
       with 20 iterations of plugin solving before Newton solving. If the plugin solving does not
       experience unusual results, then the flow goes to Newton solving, starting with solutions
       from the plugin step. Otherwise, the flow stops at the unusual plugin iteration, indicating that
       the solve setting requires further refinement:

          from sentaurus.device import *
          num_iters = 20
          move_to_newton = False

          # plugin callback
          def pcb(sim, solve):

             if not solve.info.converged:
                 solve.request_break("Stop plugin iterations. Some equations did
                                                       not converge.", keep_solution=False)

             elif solve.info.iteration > 0 and
                      solve.info.error > solve.info.error_prev:
                      solve.request_break("Stop plugin iterations due to error
                                                             increase." , keep_solution=False)

             elif solve.info.iteration == num_iters - 1 and

SentaurusTM Device User Guide                                                 1554
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface

       solve.info.error >= 1:
move_to_newton = True
solve.request_break("Plugin iterations exhausted before system

                                      converge.", keep_solution=True)

setup = SimulationSetup(...)              ...),  solver_callback=pcb)
sim = Simulation(setup)
sim.solve(Plugin(iterations=niters,
if move_to_newton:

     sim.solve(Coupled(...))

Solving and Loading the Simulation State

The solve method of the Simulation class returns an object that represents the current

state of the simulation. This object can be passed to the load method of the Simulation
class to restore the state at a later time:

...                                                         #1>))
sim = Simulation(setup)
# Do ramp #1 and keep hold of the state to restore later
state_ramp1 = sim.solve(QuasiStationary(<settings for ramp
# Now do a second ramp
sim.solve(QuasiStationary(<settings for ramp #2>))
# Restore the ramp #1 simulation state
sim.load(state_ramp1)
# Now do a third ramp
sim.solve(QuasiStationary(<settings for ramp #3>))

The SimulationState class is largely opaque and the underlying data is kept in memory,
rather than stored on disk. However, the state for individual devices is accessible as an

in-memory Tdr_Collection which can be then saved to a TDR file or passed on to other
TCAD SentaurusTM Python modules.

Creating Custom Datasets

       The Python interface to Sentaurus Device provides the DeviceSnapshot class which allows
       access to the many datasets constructed during a simulation, and these can be used to
       create custom datasets. An example used elsewhere in this user guide is that of the

      calculation of electron conductivity n = qnn . In this example, the electron conductivity
      at each vertex is a simple product of the electronic charge q , the electron density n , and
      the electron mobility n at that vertex.

       The following example demonstrates this:

          from sentaurus.device import *
          import numpy as np
          ...

SentaurusTM Device User Guide                                          1555
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
NumPy Usage

          sim = Simulation(setup)
          sim.solve(QuasiStationary(...))
          # Get the final snapshot of the simulation and construct
          # the electron conductivity
          snp = sim.result["DeviceSnapshot"].iloc[-1]
          eDensity = snp.get_dataset(Dataset.eDensity)
          eMobility = snp.get_dataset(Dataset.eMobility)
          mesh = snp.mesh
          idxs = mesh.get_vertices(material_group="Semiconductor")
          eCond = np.zeros(len(eDensity))
          eCond[idxs] = eDensity[idxs] * eMobility[idxs] * 1.602e-19
          snp.set_user_field(Dataset.PMIUserField20, eCond)

       In this example, the get_dataset method of the DeviceSnapshot class is used to access
       the datasets produced by the simulation, and the set_user_field method is used to set the
       dataset for PMIUserField20 with the result of the electron conductivity calculation.

       In addition to this, the mesh property of the DeviceSnapshot class is used to access the
       vertex indices corresponding to the semiconductor regions of the device, for which the
       electron conductivity is valid. Additional documentation about the DeviceSnapshot class
       can be viewed from the gpythonsh Python interpreter by entering help
       (sentaurus.device.DeviceSnapshot).

NumPy Usage

       The Sentaurus Device Python interface for datasets represents them as NumPy arrays, and
       this has many benefits. The NumPy Python module is a third-party Python module that has
       become widely adopted in many numeric disciplines and is immensely powerful.

       In the previous example for calculating the electron conductivity, two features of NumPy are
       utilized. The first is that elementwise array operations can be performed simply with
       standard operators. For example:

          >>> import numpy as np
          >>> a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
          >>> b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
          >>> a + b
          array([5, 7, 9])
          >>>

       This simple way of performing elementwise operations is very powerful and efficient,
       because the looping over the array is performed in optimized C code, rather than in Python.

       The second feature that is used is advanced indexing that applies operations only to certain
       elements in the arrays. For example:

          >>> import numpy as np
          >>> a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
          >>> b = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1556
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
Extracting Parameters

          >>> c = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])
          >>> idxs = [0, 3, 5]
          >>> c[idxs] = a[idxs] + b[idxs]
          >>> c
          array([ 2, 0, 0, 8, 0, 12])
          >>>

       In this example, elementwise operations are performed only for the array indices 0, 3, and
       5. This is useful for performing operations on specific mesh locations in the dataset.
       This is a brief introduction to NumPy, but a wealth of documentation and tutorials are
       available online. NumPy is also discussed in the TCAD Sentaurus Tutorial, Python
       Language module (see TCAD Sentaurus Tutorial: Simulation Projects on page 57).

Extracting Parameters

       In addition to the Sentaurus Device Python interface, the general-purpose Python shell also
       provides access to the Extraction module, which is part of the Sentaurus Visual Python
       mode svisualpylib package. As a result, you can easily analyze .plt files generated by
       Sentaurus Device and extract electrical parameters.
       The following example shows a gate ramp followed by the extraction of various electrical
       parameters such as the threshold voltage, maximum transconductance, and subthreshold
       voltage swing:

          from sentaurus.device import *

          # Run the simulation
          setup = SimulationSetup(...)
          sim = Simulation(setup)
          sim.solve(QuasiStationary(...))

          # Get the results
          res = sim.result
          vgs = res["gate OuterVoltage"]
          ids = res["drain Voltage"]

          # Extract electrical parameters
          import svisualpylib.extract as ext
          lgate = 0.25 # gate length in um
          io = 100e-9/lgate # [A/um]
          vtgm = ext.extract_vtgm(vgs, ids, name="Vtgm")
          vti = ext.extract_vti(vgs, ids, io, name='VtiLin')
          ss = ext.extract_ss(vgs, ids, v_o=0.01, name="SS")
          gm = ext.extract_gm(vgs, ids, name="gm")

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1557
W-2024.09
Chapter 41: Python Interface
Limitations

       To access the documentation for the extraction module functions:
       · From the Sentaurus Workbench GUI, choose Help > Python API Documentation >

            S-Visual.
       · From the Sentaurus Visual GUI, choose Help > Python API Reference.
       Alternatively, you can use the Python help function in gpythonsh. For example:

          import svisualpylib.extract as ext
          help(ext.extract_vtgm)

Limitations

       The Python interface uses an object-oriented methodology to define the simulation setup
       that is done in the command file. Currently, only a subset of the possible commands and
       parameters supported by the command file syntax are available in the Python interface.
       To add arbitrary command strings to any command, you can use the set_generic_command
       and set_generic_option methods. For example, to add a CurrentPlot section:

          sim = Simulation(...)
          sim.devices[""].set_generic_commands("""
          CurrentPlot{

               SRH(Integrate(Semiconductor))
          }
          """)

       Aside from that, the following general limitations also apply:
       · The creation of multiple instances of the Simulation class is not currently supported.
       · If a transient simulation is performed that calls the Simulation.solve() method

            multiple times, then the correct initial time, that is, the final time of the last transient
            statement, must be specified because Sentaurus Device does not retain the last
            transient time from the previous call to Simulation.solve().

B

BSyntax

The syntax of the command file of Sentaurus Device, and the basic syntactical and lexical
conventions are described here.

       Sentaurus Device has a hierarchical input syntax. At the lowest level, device, system, and
       solve information is specified as well as the default and global parameters. Inside each
       Device section, the parameters specific to one device type can be specified.

       Inside the System section, the real devices are specified or instantiated. Here, parameters
       can be given that are specific to one instantiation of a device. The command file is a
       collection of specifications used to establish the simulation environment with actions
       describing which equations must be solved and how they must be solved. The syntax of the
       command file contains several entry types. All basic command file entries adhere to the
       syntactical and lexical rules described in Table 198.

Table 198 Entry types in Sentaurus Device

Entry type Description

Keyword  These are the known names of the command file. They are case insensitive.
         Therefore, the following keywords are all equivalent: Quasistationary,
         QuasiStationary, and quasistationary. Most keywords can be abbreviated.
         This example can also be written as QuasiStat.

Integer  These are (possibly) signed decimal numbers. The following integers are valid: 123,
         -73492, 0

Float    Floating-point numbers are compatible with the C language format for floating-point
         numbers. The following floating-point numbers are valid: 123, 123.0, 1.23e2,
         -1.23E2

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1565
W-2024.09
Appendix B: Syntax

Table 198 Entry types in Sentaurus Device (Continued)

Entry type Description

Vector              Vectors in real space are defined depending on the actual dimension as follows:
                    · In three dimensions, a vector is specified by three floating-point numbers.
String              · In two dimensions, a vector is specified by two floating-point numbers enclosed
Identifier
Assignment             in parentheses. The floating-point numbers are separated by commas or space.
Signal              · In one dimension, one floating-point number without parentheses is sufficient.
List                Valid vectors are (1,0,2), (1e-4,-1e-3), and 1.

Structured          Strings are delimited by quotation marks. They are compatible with the C language
entries             format for strings. The following strings are valid: "Vdd", "output/diode"

                    These are used to name objects such as nodes, devices, or attributes. They are
                    compatible with the C language format for identifiers. The following identifiers are
                    valid: Vdd, diode, bjt_345

                    These are used to set values to keywords. Therefore, the following are valid
                    assignments: Digits=4, Save="output/diode"

                    Signals are time dependent, piecewise, linear functions (not to be confused with
                    UNIX signals) that are defined as inputs on the contacts of a device. They are
                    specified as follows: (value0 at time0, value1 at time1, ...value_n at time_n). The
                    following signal is valid: (0 at 0, 1 at 10.0e-9, 1 at 20.0e-9)

                    Lists are collections of keywords, assignments, and complex entries. They are
                    delimited by "(...)" or "{...}". The following lists are valid:
                    { Number=0 Voltage=0

                       Voltage=( 0 at 0, 0 at 2e-8 ) }
                    { Method=Super Digits=6 Numerically }
                    ( MinStep=1e-15 InitialStep=1e-10 Digits=3 )

                    These are parameterized definitions or commands that can have the forms
                    <keyword> {<keywords>}, <keyword> (<keywords>), or <keyword> (<list>)
                    {<list>}.

CFile-Naming Conventions

This appendix describes the file-naming conventions for TCAD tools relevant to Sentaurus
Device.

File Extensions

       All strings that represent file names containing a dot (.) within their base name are taken
       literally. Otherwise, Sentaurus Device extends the given strings with the appropriate
       extension.

       Sentaurus Device expands the extensions for output files by its tool extension _des, for
       example, the extension of a saved file is _des.sav.

       During transient, quasistationary, and continuation simulations, the plot and save files are
       numbered by a global index.

D

DCommand-Line Options

This appendix lists the most useful command-line options available in Sentaurus Device.

Starting Sentaurus Device

       To start Sentaurus Device, enter:

          sdevice [<options>] [<commandfile>]

       Sentaurus Device appends automatically the corresponding extension to the given
       command file if necessary. If no command file is specified, Sentaurus Device reads from
       standard input.

Command-Line Options

       Sentaurus Device interprets the following options:

Option                         Description

-d                             Prints debug information into the debug file. The information printed
                               includes the numeric values of the Jacobian and RHS for each
                               equation at each solution step.

-h                             Lists these options and exits.

-i                             Prints the initial solution in the save file, and print files specified in
                               the File section of the command file, and exits without performing
                               further computations.

-L                             Writes the silicon model parameters into the file Silicon.par and
                               exits.

-L <commandfile>               Writes model parameter files for all the materials, material
                               interfaces, and electrodes used in <commandfile> and exits.

ERuntime Statistics

This appendix presents information about obtaining runtime statistics from Sentaurus

Generating Statistics

The command sdevicestat displays some statistics of a previous run of Sentaurus Device
based on the information found in its log file. For example, the command:

 sdevicestat test_des.log

generates the following statistics:

Total number of Newton         iterations    : 8
Number of restarts             above times)  : 0
Rhs-time                                     : 9.19 % ( 38.80 s )
Jacobian-time                                : 1.43 % ( 6.05 s )
Solve-time                                   : 88.76 % ( 374.70 s )
Overhead                                     : 0.62 % ( 2.61 s )
Total CPU time (sum of                       : 422.16 s

The sdevicestat command recognizes whether the WallClock keyword has been
specified in the Math section of the Sentaurus Device command file (see Parallelization on
page 241). In this case, the same simulation on a dual processor machine produces the

following output:

Total number of Newton iterations            : 8
Number of restarts                           : 0
Rhs-time                                     : 8.57 % ( 20.68 s )

FData Names and Plot Names

This appendix provides information about data names and plot names.

Table 200, Table 201, Table 202, and Table 203 list the data names as they appear in the
TDR and PLT files, and that are available in the current plot PMI (see Current Plot File on
page 1489).

The plot names that are recognized in a Plot or CurrentPlot section of Sentaurus Device
are identical to the data names if not mentioned otherwise (see Device Plots on page 191).

Vector data can be plotted by appending /Vector to the corresponding keyword. For
example:

 Plot { ElectricField/Vector }

Element-based scalar data can be plotted by appending /Element to the corresponding
keyword. For example:

 Plot { eMobility/Element }

Special vector data can be plotted by appending /SpecialVector to the corresponding
keyword. For example:

 Plot { eSHEDistribution/SpecialVector }

Tensor data can be plotted by appending /Tensor to the corresponding keyword. For
example:

 Plot { Stress/Tensor }

Note:
    The location rivertex refers to region-interface vertices.

For the kinetic Monte Carlo metal-insulator-metal (MIM) transport capability, Table 204 lists
the plot name that is recognized in the Plot section of a Sentaurus Device command file for
saving particle data related to MIM defects.

A dynamic dataset is a special type of data that encapsulates multiple related datasets
under a common dataset name. In Table 200, each data name defines a unique type of data;

G

GCommand File Overview

This appendix presents an overview of the command file of Sentaurus Device.

Top Level of Command File on page 1616 presents the topmost level of the command file.
Use this table to obtain a top-down overview of the command file. The remaining sections
are ordered alphabetically. Headings of tables, therein, mostly start with a keyword. Use
these tables to find details about keywords.

Organization of Command File Overview

       The tables in this appendix have two or three columns, and their rows are ordered
       alphabetically with respect to the first (and, as far as applicable, the middle) column.
       Placeholders (cross references, user-supplied values in angle brackets (<>)) precede
       explicit keywords, irrespective of alphabetic order.

       The left column contains keywords that can appear in the command file. In the topmost rows
       of some tables, the left column references another table. This means that all keywords in the
       referenced table can appear in the referring table as well. Some keywords are followed by
       an opening parenthesis or an opening brace to indicate that the keyword expects a selection
       of options listed in the middle column of the current and the following rows.

       The middle column contains options or values to the keyword in the left column, one per row.
       For a selection of options, the last row indicates the closing parenthesis or the closing brace.
       For some tables, the middle column would be empty and is omitted.

       The right column contains the description of keywords, options, and values of the row. As far
       as applicable, the right column also provides the following additional information:

       · The default value, which can be:

            An explicit value. Those values are written in Courier font, as you would type them.

            + or - to indicate the default (true or false, respectively) for keywords that support the
                - prefix.

            on or off for keywords that set and reset flags, but do not support the - prefix.

SentaurusTM Device User Guide  1614
W-2024.09
Appendix G: Command File Overview
Organization of Command File Overview

            An asterisk (*) to indicate the default among mutually exclusive alternatives.

            An exclamation mark (!) if no default exists and you must specify a value.

      · The unit assumed for the given quantity. In unit specifications, d denotes the dimension

           of the mesh. For dimensionless quantities, no unit is specified.

       · The location for which keywords should be specified, given as characters in
           parentheses:

            (g) stands for global parameters that must not appear in region-specific,
                interface-specific, or contact-specific sections.

            (r) stands for region-specific (or material-specific) parameters that usually do not
                make sense when specified for interfaces or contacts.

            (c) and (i) stand for contact-specific or interface-specific parameters.

       Furthermore, the tables use the following conventions:

       · An ellipsis (...) denotes that the preceding item can be repeated an arbitrary number of
           times.

       · An asterisk (*) followed by an integer, both typeset in Times font, denotes that the
           preceding item must appear the given number of times.

       · Optional components of specifications are enclosed in brackets, and the brackets are not
           part of the syntax.

       · Angle brackets (<>) indicate user-supplied values. Table 205 summarizes the common
           types of specification. More specific notation is explained in the last column of the table
           where it is used.

       Some tables use additional conventions as necessary. They are explained in the text that
       precedes the respective table.

Table 205 Notation for user-supplied values

Specification    Description

<(x,y)> <[x,y]>  Range of floating-point numbers from x to y. Parentheses are used when
<(x,y]> <[x,y)>  the limits are excluded from the range; brackets are used when they are
                 included. To denote ranges unbound on one side, the corresponding limit is
                 omitted.

<carrier>        A carrier type, Electron or Hole.

<float>          A floating-point number (integers are special cases thereof).

Specification   Description

<ident>         An identifier. This is like a string, but is not enclosed in double quotation
                marks.

<int>           An integer.
<n..m>
                A range of integers, from n to m, inclusively. Either n or m can be omitted, to
                denote ranges that are unbound on one side.

<string>        A sequence of characters (including digits and special characters) included
                in double quotation marks. Unlike most Sentaurus Device input, strings are
                case sensitive.

<vector>        A sequence of up to three floating-point numbers, enclosed in parentheses,
<System_Coord>  and separated by spaces. For example: (1.0 3 0)
                CrystalSystem or SimulationSystem.
